title: DfE Decoded #164: What the Looked-After Children Data Tells Us About Stability
author: Paul Urry
source: paulurry68.substack.com (DfE Decoded, A Headteacher's Perspective), October 18, 2026
summary: Paul Urry reads the technical 2026/27 children looked-after data return guidance and finds a consistent theme underneath the coding rules: stability. The main change is a new module recording Deprivation of Liberty Orders, but he argues the bigger story is that the system now tracks placement, school and social worker stability, and the reasons behind moves. He notes that for the child these are one experience, a new home, school and adult, rebuilt repeatedly, and that school can sometimes be the most stable part of a looked-after child's life. He also covers missing episodes, the Strengths and Difficulties Questionnaire, tracking of care leavers to age 25 and the participation of children in their reviews. He cautions that a better dataset does not create a better childhood, because children experience the system one relationship at a time. For school leaders he suggests asking which looked-after pupils have recently experienced change, counting how many adults each child deals with, and treating stability as an educational issue.
points: The return now tracks placement, school and social worker stability together, which matches how a looked-after child actually experiences instability.
The reasons for a move matter more than the count, because three placement moves can describe planned progress for one child and repeated breakdown for another.
A sudden change in a child's behaviour in school may reflect a placement move, a new social worker or a review decision that the school does not know about.
School can offer continuity through the same adults, routines and expectations when little else in a child's life is stable.
Urry cautions that data can show where instability is happening but cannot create stability, which only people can provide.
quotes: But underneath all the coding, dates and reporting rules is a much more interesting picture of what the system is trying to understand about children in care. And the word that keeps coming back is stability.
A new home. A new school. A new adult. A new story to explain. A new set of relationships to rebuild.
A child with three placement moves has not necessarily had the same experience as another child with three placement moves.
When that person changes, the child can end up explaining themselves again. And again. And again.
But perhaps the most powerful thing school can sometimes offer is continuity.
A child who suddenly becomes dysregulated may not have suddenly “developed behaviour problems”. Something may have changed.
The data can tell us where instability is happening. It cannot create stability. People do that.
What are we doing to make school the most stable part of this child’s life?
